# On the Strange Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking about boredom lately—that restless, fidgety feeling we all try to escape. We reach for phones, fill silence with podcasts, schedule every moment. But what if boredom is actually a gift we're rejecting?

When you're bored, your mind isn't being hijacked by stimulation. It wanders. And wandering minds are where ideas live. Some of humanity's best thoughts probably happened while someone was staring out a window, waiting for water to boil, or lying in bed unable to sleep.

I notice my best ideas don't come when I'm frantically searching for them. They arrive unbidden during mundane moments—showering, walking, doing dishes. There's something about the absence of external stimulation that lets the internal machinery actually work.

We're so afraid of being alone with our thoughts that we've engineered boredom almost completely out of modern life. But loneliness and boredom aren't the same thing. Boredom is actually a sign of freedom—you have time and space that isn't allocated. That's increasingly rare.

The irony is that we pursue productivity and stimulation hoping to feel fulfilled, yet the constant input leaves us oddly empty. We're fed but not nourished.

I'm not romanticizing boredom—it can be genuinely uncomfortable. But maybe that discomfort is useful. Maybe it's the feeling of your mind shifting gears, clearing space, preparing to create.

What would happen if we stopped treating boredom as an enemy and started treating it as an invitation?
